【シンシナティ（米オハイオ州）16日（日本時間17日）＝横山尚杜】米大リーグ、ドジャースの佐々木朗希投手（24）がレッズ戦の試合前にライブBP（実戦形式の打撃練習）に登板。「右手中指のまめ」で負傷者リスト（IL）入り後、2度目で4回50球を消化した。レッズ戦に先発したスネルが「左股関節の張り」を訴え、1回19球で緊急降板。ポストシーズンの先発に暗雲が立ち込め、佐々木は復帰戦で先発する見込みとなった。
地区優勝が手に届く直前で、アクシデント続きだ。ドジャースは先発したスネルが1回19球で緊急降板。既往歴4度の「左股関節の張り」を訴え、次回登板が白紙。ポストシーズン（PS）に黄色信号が灯った。一方、「右手中指のまめ」から復帰目前の佐々木は、試合前のライブBPで4回50球を消化。救援転向が濃厚な状況から一気に風向きが変わった。
「ロウキは今週末のジャイアンツ戦では先発しないと思う。ただ、彼の次の登板は先発になると思う」
試合後のロバーツ監督は佐々木の復帰戦が先発になる見込みだと明言。当初は山本由伸、スクバル、スネル、グラスノーでPS先発枠は満席だったが、空席が出る可能性が浮上。この日の佐々木は患部に公式戦でも使用可能なダーマボンド（皮膚接着剤）を患部に施し、球威抜群の速球を投げ込んだ。
ドジャースはスネル緊急降板で、救援陣をつぎ込むも敗戦。地区優勝マジック「1」で迎えたが、自力で決められず2位パドレスも勝利したため、敵地に用意されたシャンパンの封は閉ざされたままとなった。17日（同18日）レッズ戦で勝利するか、パドレスがロッキーズに敗れた時点で5年連続の地区優勝が決定する。
「彼は重要な存在になる」。ロバーツ監督は佐々木をポストシーズンのキーマンに挙げた。後半戦は内容のある投球を見せていた矢先のアクシデントだった。シーズン最終週で、2年連続のPSに弾みをつける。

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are on track to win the NL West and probably earn a first-round bye in the postseason. That comes despite a recent onslaught of injuries. Los Angeles is not unaccustomed to a stacked injury list, but the Dodgers' elite depth — aided by a top-ranked farm system and unrivalred spending power — makes them uniquely resilient.
What has helped L.A. win back-to-back World Series titles, however, is their knack for getting healthy at the right time and charging into October at full strength. The Dodgers are hoping to do just that, again. Let's rank six potential returners who could make an outsized impact.
6. RHP Edwin Díaz
Should Edwin Díaz actually come back for the playoffs? He got rocked in his recent Triple-A rehab appearance. The Dodgers' prized $69 million investment has only pitched 13.2 innings in the majors this season, with a disastrous 11.85 ERA (not a typo). Díaz has not looked right at any point.
While the Dodgers presumably want such an expensive and accomplished reliever on the postseason roster, it may be smarter to punt on this season entirely. Díaz is more than capable of rebuilding confidence and getting healthy in the offseason, but it's unclear if L.A. can rely on him in even the lowest-leverage spots currently. Rather than playing with fire, so to speak, the Dodgers should probably lean on their spectacular bullpen depth and keep Díaz on the sidelines. The risk far outweighs the potential reward of rushing him back.
That said, when healthy, Díaz has a long track record as one of MLB's best closers. We know he can electify in the late innings. If the Dodgers are confident for reasons we on the outside aren't privy too, never say never on a triumphant turnaround.
5. RHP Roki Sasaki
Through two seasons, the Rōki Sasaki experience has not quite lived up to expectations for Dodgers fans. Hailed as the best Japanese pitching prospect in a generation, the 24-year-old looks an awful lot like... a prospect. A work in progress. Los Angeles expected immediate results. Now, the Dodgers are hoping Sasaki can iron out command issues against MLB competition. He appeared briefly in the minors this season, but the Dodgers are effectively all-in on Sasaki as a major league pitcher.
Sasaki is expected to recover from a blister before the playoffs, although the Dodgers are uncertain about his exact role. The rotation is much too deep for Sasaki to start in a must-win environment. He was effectively L.A.'s closer last October — a role in which he thrived — but a healthy Tanner Scott removes Sasaki from consideration for that role. Expect him in the bullpen, probably handling bulk work if one of L.A.'s starters is forced out early.
4. C Dalton Rushing
Dalton Rushing was recently returned to the IL after suffering a setback in his recovery from UCL surgery. He's done catching for the season, but L.A. still hopes the 25-year-old can return as a hitter. Of course, if Rushing is effectively relegated to DH, it will be hard to get him in the lineup with Shohei Ohtani also on the roster. Rushing could end up as a situational, pinch-hitter type in October, if he's even on the roster.
It's a credit to how deep the Dodgers are that Rushing being "situational," rather than essential, is even in the cards. The rookie backstop cooled off after the All-Star break, but he's still phenomenally talented. He has a .798 OPS and 120 wRC+ as a rookie, with 12 home runs in only 250 at-bats.
Rushing is stuck behind Will Smith on the org chart, which complicates his future somewhat, but the Dodgers will find ways to use him if he's available.
3. RHP Edgardo Henriquez
The Dodgers hope Edgardo Henriquez can return from a low-grade back strain come the playoffs. The 24-year-old fireballer has quickly established himself as one of baseball's most dominant relievers. He has a 2.85 ERA and 1.03 WHIP with 71 strikeouts in 60.0 innings pitched this season; he ranks in MLB's 99th percentile for both hard-hit rate (27.1 percent) and average fastball velo (100.8 mph).
Henriquez is more than a hard-thrower. He misses barrels and limits explosive hits, able to force groundballs or lifeless bloopers just as often as he forces swing-and-miss. He leans heavily on his four-seam and sinker combo, with a sweeping slider that leaves opposing hitters gasping for air (.191 xwOBA). Should Henriquez return in time, the Dodgers can plug him right into high-leverage spots and expect results. He's the real deal, folks.
2. OF Andy Pages
Andy Pages is back in the batting cage after breaking his hand in mid-August. The Dodgers' centerfielder has enjoyed a proper breakout campaign, posting a .797 OPS and 119 wRC+ with elite defensive metrics and 12 stolen bases. In terms of fWAR, or wins above replacement, Pages ranks third among L.A. positional players (3.9), behind only Shohei Ohtani (6.8) and Max Muncy (4.0).
The Dodgers really need Pages on cleanup duty in centerfield. He covers so much ground and features a killer arm, which wipes runs off the board. Pages' bat cooled down before the injury, but he's still far more dangerous than L.A.'s alternatives — although the recent promotion of top prospect Josue De Paula does create a difficult decision for manager Dave Roberts, assuming the DH spot reverts back to Ohtani.
Speaking of which...
1. DH Shohei Ohtani
This was obvious, yeah? Shohei Ohtani is currently on ice as he attempts to shed bicep and knee problems. That said, the Dodgers plan to get him back before the regular season ends — and it would be absolutely shocking if Ohtani weren't leading off in Game 1 of the Dodgers' first postseason series.
The nagging nature of Ohtani's injuries mean he won't take the mound again in 2026, but he's still the most valuable hitter in the majors, on balance. Yes, Yordan Álvarez and Pete Crow-Armstrong are enjoying better seasons, but Ohtani is the man you want at the plate in a big spot. Drafting a fantasy team, he's your No. 1 pick. So on and so forth.
After spending the early portion of his MLB career on an unserious Angels team, Ohtani is two-for-two in the World Series since joining the Dodgers. He has consistently come up large in the playoffs. Assuming Ohtani is anywhere close to 100 percent, the Dodgers are once again (easy) favorites to win it all.

item.content:encoded:
In the last moment before fury overtakes calm, Tarik Skubal stands on the plateau of a 10-inch-tall pedestal of dirt and clay as an imposing and finely calibrated 240 pounds of human pitching machinery. Nothing superfluous. Nothing without purpose. Brutally efficient.
The calibrations that lead him to the mound for a playoff game are no different than for a midseason start. The pulses of electromagnetic waves over his body, the four shots of espresso, the hot tub, the peanut butter and jelly sandwich, the dynamic warmup, the 17 to 22 pitches in the bullpen ... all of it as detailed, immutable and unassailable as Newton’s second law of motion. Skubal is so detail-obsessed that he tracks the speed of the bar when he lifts weights.
“I’m always monitoring everything,” he says. “I’m making sure that I’m doing the right things to where my body is ready to go and my nervous system is ready to go out there and pitch. It’s very complex, but it’s also simple. Everything that I do has a plan. There is always a reason for everything. I don’t do anything just mindlessly.”
All of it is done so that when it comes time for the catcher to transmit the audio signal for one of Skubal’s five pitches, Skubal is good with whatever is the choice.
The planning, scheming and studying are over. It is time to accelerate particles with ferocious force. Skubal is the only pitcher on the planet who can throw 100 mph and get hitters to miss his changeup almost half the time, the highest whiff rate on the pitch among such flamethrowers who have thrown it at least 300 times. He owns both ends of the speed spectrum.
“I’m just going to go out there and compete and try to execute pitches, so I let the catchers call what they see,” he says. “There’s a lot more stuff going on cerebrally with catchers than with me when I’m on the mound. When I’m on the mound, it’s just, get the pitch. Whatever it is, execute the pitch. I don’t really want to be thinking about too much.
“The time in between starts? I’m thinking about stuff. The time in between innings? I’m thinking about stuff. But when I’m out there, I want my process to be pretty simple.”
“If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants.”
The quote is attributable to Isaac Newton in 1675, though it might be appropriated these days by Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman. While the state of starting pitching declines—starters last postseason threw fewer innings than relievers and this regular season just 57% of innings—Friedman has assembled the most expensive rotation in postseason history, if not the most decorated. He did so by seizing from other teams six elite arms whose fastballs average between 95 and 98 mph.
Dodger Stadium, ever resplendent in its timeless mid-century vibe, is home to a style of pitching that also is a throwback. Los Angeles won the World Series last year by pulling from the catalog of Koufax and Drysdale. Dodgers starters threw 10 quality starts in the 2025 postseason, the most by a world champion since the 2010 Giants. Contrary to the prevailing bullpen-heavy approach, the Los Angeles starters won postseason games, not just managed them. They were 9–4 with a 2.68 ERA. Only the 1998 Yankees and 2007 Red Sox rotations won more games in this era of expanded postseasons. The rest of MLB postseason starters last year were 13–25.
The Los Angeles aces are back, and then some. To his Ocean’s Eleven of rotations—marquee-worthy names everywhere—Friedman on Aug. 1 added Skubal, the two-time defending American League Cy Young Award winner, in a heist of a trade with the Tigers. In a span of 32 months, through free agency and trades, Friedman acquired Shohei Ohtani, Tyler Glasnow, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Roki Sasaki and Skubal. They represent six regular-season and postseason MVP awards, four Cy Young Awards and $1.38 billion in salaries, or about what it cost to pay half the players in the majors in 2011.
In the Big Four of Skubal, Yamamoto, Snell and Ohtani, the Dodgers have acquired four of the five pitchers with the lowest ERA in baseball over the past four years (minimum 50 starts), with only the Pirates’ Paul Skenes having evaded their clutches. In their combined postseason careers, the Big Four are 18–8 with a 2.85 ERA.
As L.A. attempts to become the first team in National League history to win three straight World Series, the prevailing question of this postseason is not just, Can anybody beat the Dodgers? It is, Can anybody beat the Dodgers’ starters?
“For us it’s always been ideal to go into any October with the best starting pitching you can,” Friedman says. “If there are 150-plus starting pitchers with injuries, there are certainly not 30 number ones and an abundance of ones and twos. So, there’s scarcity there. This has been a perfect storm for us being able to access so many top-end talented arms in one moment in time.”
The Dodgers’ plan this postseason is a lather-rinse-repeat exercise of last October. They conserve innings from their starters in the regular season so they can turn them loose in the highest stakes games. When L.A. faced elimination in the World Series last year, for instance, down three games to two on the road to Toronto, manager Dave Roberts used seven pitchers over the final two games, all of whom started multiple times during the regular season. Game 7 was an embarrassment of riches. Roberts used six pitchers, including Ohtani, Glasnow, Snell and Yamamoto—$1.34 billion worth of pitchers in one game, with future Hall of Famer Clayton Kershaw warming in the bullpen. Yamamoto and Snell each threw more than 525 pitches in the postseason, the first pair of World Series–winning teammates to carry such a load since Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling for the 2001 Diamondbacks.
“The thought for me has never wavered,” Friedman says of building championship teams around starting pitching. “There is more appreciation for that now because there aren’t enough of those starters—the ones you can give the ball to and feel confident they will give you six or seven innings. It’s just important to be realistic with your personnel. In ’24, with the injuries to our starting pitching, our relievers were really good. The group was deep, and we leaned on our bullpen more. In ’25, our relievers were kind of going through it a little bit and our starters were rolling. And we leaned on that. I think it’s having an appreciation for what your strengths are going into October and doing the best you can to leverage it.”
The Dodgers are a modern dynasty. They are headed to a 13th straight full season with more than 90 wins. Twelve division titles in the past 13 years. Five of the past nine NL pennants. Three of the past six World Series titles. And yet before this season began Friedman, who took over as president of baseball ops in October 2014, called this the most talented team of them all. Privately, he yearned for one more player.
“We looked to do everything we could over the offseason to avoid being a buyer in July, short of a real impact-type talent,” he says. “And so, from our standpoint, our buy side list was Tarik Skubal. End of list.”
Detroit unwittingly cooperated. The Tigers went 6–22 in May, the second-worst May in franchise history. They played themselves into shopping Skubal, a free agent after the season, before the Aug. 3 deadline. President of baseball operations Scott Harris began exploratory talks with teams about Skubal in the week before the deadline. On July 31, Friedman says, “I went to sleep and I would have thought there was no chance that the deal would wrap the next day.”
The next morning, Harris and Friedman spoke again. Later in the afternoon, everything suddenly changed. Harris wanted final offers. He would present them to the Tigers’ ownership, and they would pick the winning bid within hours. According to one executive, the Dodgers sent signals they were in parallel discussions with the Mariners for pitcher George Kirby, a word on the street seen as a gambit to raise the pressure on Detroit. Friedman, however, denies that scenario. Skubal, he reiterates, was the only name on his shopping list. “If we were fortunate enough to wind up with him, great,” Friedman says. “If not, we weren’t out in the market looking for pitching.”
Friedman put three players in the package for Skubal, none of whom would hurt the Dodgers’ current and near-term plans: River Ryan, a soon-to-turn 28-year-old pitcher coming off Tommy John surgery; Double A outfielder Zyhir Hope, 21; and Class A pitcher Brady Smith, also 21. Harris accepted.
The package was a testament to the Dodgers’ treasure-hunting expertise, the secret sauce underneath their vast spending power. Ryan, a former 11th-round pick, was plucked from the Padres for Matt Beaty, a utility player and former 12th-round pick. Hope was another former 11th-round pick swiped from the Cubs when the Dodgers needed to move first baseman Michael Busch. Smith was the 95th player picked in the 2023 draft. The Dodgers turned straw into gold. And Skubal says he immediately felt comfortable changing teams for the first time, in this case to a franchise known for its abundant resources, including two team planes, one for players only.
“I mean, all the amenities are first class, you know?” he says. “All the recovery modalities, all the spaces they have, the way they treat the families, the family room ... I mean, they’re unreal.
“It’s awesome to be a part of something where the standard is winning a World Series. That’s the way everybody goes about their business, from ownership to president to GM to manager to players, and then you talk about support staff and the chefs in the kitchen, the flight attendants ... They all go out of their way to make sure you have everything you need to go out there and perform. I feel like everyone in this organization is rowing in the same direction and everybody wants a World Series just as bad as the players do.”
Says Friedman, “He has been awesome. He has seamlessly fit into the group. He has gone out of his way to try to forge relationships with teammates and staff. He is very convicted in his prep work, but also really curious.”
Skubal rocketed to an elite pitching level in 2023 with the help of a 3-D printer. The lefthander always had trouble mastering a changeup because his hand more easily supinates than pronates, meaning he lacked the natural forearm and wrist action that creates sink and fade by letting the baseball slip from his ring and pinkie fingers as the thumb turns down. Tigers pitching coaches Chris Fetter and Robin Lund introduced him to the concept of seam-shifted wake, the uneven airflow the raised seams create over a baseball. A pitcher without natural pronation can still deaden the baseball and create movement by harnessing these aerodynamics.
Lund, a former associate professor of kinesiology with a PhD in exercise science, had been hired that season from the University of Iowa. He had the Tigers use a 3-D printer to create a plastic mold that cradles half a baseball. The mold had a circular opening that let Lund draw a black dot with a Sharpie inside the horseshoe of the seams. “Keep the dot on top of the baseball,” he told Skubal, “and think about cutting across the face of the ball.”
When Skubal throws a baseball in that manner, the air catches the seams in a way that sinks and fades his changeup like a traditional changeup but without the pronation. Over the past four seasons, Skubal’s seam-shifted pitch ranks as the best changeup in baseball, according to Run Value among pitchers with at least 1,000 changeups. (Snell’s changeup is ranked No. 2.)
“Every once in a while, when I feel a little off, I’ll get it marked up and go right back to it,” Skubal says of the dotted training baseball. “But I haven’t done that in a while. It’s more just been about pitch execution, not pitch shape right now.”
The wonder of Skubal is that the game’s best changeup pitcher over those same four years also has the No. 3-ranked four-seam fastball among starting pitchers who have thrown at least 1,500 of that pitch. (Ohtani and Yamamoto rank Nos. 1 and 2.) With his natural supination, Skubal throws his fastball with a spin axis equivalent to the hour hand of a clock pointing to 11:15. “I throw a heater that’s not 100% efficient,” he says. “When it is 100% efficient, it’s actually a worse pitch. I need to cut it a little bit. I need to get like 94%, 92% efficiency because then I get more ride and a little bit more cut.”
Changeups and four-seamers account for 61% of his pitches. Sinkers, sliders and curveballs complete his arsenal, unless you include the adrenalin that makes him one of the most ferociously aggressive pitchers. Skubal has ranked first or second in first-pitch strike percentage two years running.
“The game is as analytic as ever,” he says. “You do want to get scouting reports and all that stuff. You can get as deep as you want, but for me it’s really about first-pitch strikes. It’s winning your 1–1 counts. It’s getting to two-strike counts as fast as possible because when you’re in those moments, you have the most leverage ever.
“When you get into two-strike counts, you should have all the confidence in the world. You’ve worked your ass off to get to this count. Now I’ve given myself room to get out of the zone a little bit. And sometimes I challenge guys in the zone, too, because when you get into count leverage, you have everything. Just execute a pitch, and the guy’s out.”
Skubal’s adrenalin-laced, pedal-to-the-floor style of pitching is well-suited for the postseason, in which he has made six career starts, all on the road and all with only two or three runs of support. Among the 219 pitchers who have made at least six starts in postseason history, Skubal ranks first in strikeouts per nine innings (12.7), second in WHIP (0.731) and third in hits per nine innings (5.2) and strikeouts per walk (9.33). His 2.04 postseason ERA is the lowest ever by a pitcher never to reach the World Series (minimum 35 innings).
“I love it,” he says of the postseason. “I feed off environments and energy and stadiums all in a positive way. The average velocity on the heater goes up. All the shapes kind of go up. The execution gets a little bit better, too.”
Come October, the calibrations that prepare him for the mound will not change. Skubal will stick to his mission-control like pre-launch routine:
• T-minus 150 minutes: Training room treatment with pulsed electromagnetic field therapy to relieve any soreness and stimulate blood flow.
• T-minus 120 minutes: Four shots of espresso. “That way,” he says, “I’m heavily caffeinated and ready to go.”
• T-minus 115 minutes: Hot tub followed by stretching and general body warmup.
• T-minus 60 minutes: Peanut butter and jelly sandwich. “Always Uncrustables,” he says. “[An] Uncrustable right to a toaster is the best thing in the world. They’re so convenient and they have them everywhere. And I know my stomach handles them well, so that’s why I eat them.”
• T-minus 40 minutes: Dynamic warmup to raise heart rate and body temperature.
• T-minus 30 minutes: Play catch.
• T-minus 20 minutes: Warm up on bullpen mound. “It always ends up being 17 to 22 pitches,” he says. “Seventeen to 22 throws is all it really takes for me.”
• T-minus eight minutes: Last bullpen pitch. Walk to dugout.
• T-minus one minute: A last reminder.
“The main thing that I remind myself in bigger moments is the game still stays the game,” he says. “The bigger the moment, the simpler the process needs to be. Just go do the things that make you great ... the first-pitch strikes, getting ahead, throwing strikes, getting into leverage, and getting these guys out early and often and putting them on their toes as much as you can. So, the bigger the game, the simpler my game gets on the mound.”
Skubal will stand on that plateau with his hands in front of his chest. The catcher will give him the radio-transmitted signal for the pitch. Skubal, who wears only the receiving device, not a transmitter, inevitably will agree. There is little mystery what is coming. Skubal threw a fastball on the first pitch of 153 of his 159 career starts through mid-August, postseason included.
With the ball in his glove, he will raise his hands in front of his face, peering over his mitt like a marksman through a sight. With a sidestep of his right leg, Skubal rocks his hands down to his belt. It is the quiet trigger to a delivery so violent and explosive that it is as if a starburst of fireworks shoots off 100 times a night. The right leg lifts so high his toes reach eye height. As he strides down the mound, he so separates the ball from his glove with straightened arms he seems to be stretching a giant rubber band to its breaking point. The glove points toward the upper deck, flashed to the hitter like a magician’s diversion. His shoulders are severely slanted, as if throwing a javelin.
Where is the baseball? It is low and behind him. It is as if he is reaching back. Reaching back all the way to Octobers past, when starting pitchers were the Hercules of the postseason, demigods who would squint against the flash-pops of the Graflex Speed Graphics in the pregame phalanx of photographers who posed them like heavyweight fighters. They were the stone and mortar of which championships were built.
“Starters,” Skubal says, “set the tone for everything going on. Yeah, I think that’s why teams win.”
Skubal and the Dodgers are reaching back to such an era. Whether four, five or six deep, they are the only team that can play such a style every postseason game they play. In the Big Four, the Dodgers could send a multiple Cy Young Award winner or a postseason MVP to the mound every night of October. Their methodology is as intentional as Skubal’s calibrations. Who will stop them?
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. Blake Snell exits Dodgers’ loss early because of injury
- Click here to listen to this article
-
CINCINNATI — The trouble started as Dodgers left-hander Blake Snell threw in the Great American Ball Park bullpen before the game.
“I felt good all day, and then the second-to-last pitch of the bullpen, I threw a slider and then I felt it grab,” Snell said of the groin tightness that ended up taking him out of the Dodgers’ 6-2 loss to the Reds early. “So I was like, ‘Alright, let’s see what we can do.’”
With Snell guiding the ball without driving hard off his back leg, his velocity was down a tick or two through a 19-pitch first inning. He gave up one hit, a single to Sal Stewart, which he quickly erased with a successful pick-off that caught Stewart in an inning-ending run-down.
“I was going to try to get through five [innings],” he said, “but I just knew I didn’t really have a good shot at doing that and remaining healthy.”
In a conversation with manager Dave Roberts, pitching coach Mark Prior and head athletic trainer Thomas Albert, they all agreed the best course of action would be to pull Snell from the game. Right-handed reliever Blake Treinen replaced him in the second inning.
With only 10 games left in the season, it’s unclear when Snell will be ready to pitch again.
“The next couple days are really going to decide,” Snell said. “But I’d love to throw on my next [scheduled start day]. Either there or a couple days after. But definitely, I want to try to get one more in the regular season.”
Teoscar Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday in the Dodgers’ win against the Reds was his second home run in as many nights.
The Dodgers’ loss marked Snell’s eighth start of the season. His 2026 debut was delayed by shoulder fatigue. And then after one start, he landed back on the injured list to undergo arthroscopic surgery to remove loose bodies from his left elbow.
Since returning, he hasn’t given up more than one run in a start. Through Wednesday, Snell has a 1.86 ERA. And he’s a key member of the Dodgers’ projected postseason rotation.
“I don’t think anyone can sit here right now and say what’s going to happen in the next week to 10 days,” Roberts said, noting that the team would decide whether to send him to get imaging after they returned to Los Angeles. “It’s under the, ‘I’m glad it’s not worse and we caught it early’ [category].”
Snell has a history of left groin and adductor strains. He spent time on the IL in 2021, 2022 and 2024 for such injuries. He said this injury didn’t feel nearly as severe as any of those.
“[In the past] I felt like that and then I kept pitching on two of them and strained both of them,” he said. “One was a grade one, one was a grade two. So I’m definitely happy I stopped. … I’m aware if I kept pitching, I definitely would’ve strained it. So for me to stop, that’s a first. Maybe I’m growing up. I don’t know. But that was definitely the right move. And next couple days, we’ll see where we’re at and go from there. But I think I’ll be good to go.”
The last couple years, in an effort to avoid another groin strain, Snell has incorporated Copenhagen planks into his routine, strengthening the area.
“I thought I had this thing figured out,” Snell said. “Well, technically, I still do. I didn’t strain it, so that was a good thing. … I haven’t felt it at all until that pitch in the bullpen, and I was just kind of thrown off by it. So I’ve done what I’ve needed to do to be strong and healthy. Definitely a shock to me.”
After Snell left the game, the Dodgers used six relievers to get through seven innings. They combined to give up six runs and 12 hits, including a pair of home runs.
Left-hander Kris Bubic, acquired at the trade deadline while on the IL (flexor strain, shoulder impingement), made his Dodgers debut in the eighth inning. In his first major-league appearance since mid-May, he allowed an infield single and recorded two strikeouts in a scoreless inning.
The Dodgers missed a chance to clinch the division with a win. And the Padres beat the Rockies on Wednesday to keep the division race mathematically alive.
So, the Dodgers will get another shot at champagne showers in Cincinnati Wednesday when left-hander Justin Wrobleski takes the mound. The Dodgers optioned right-hander Bobby Miller after his 2 ⅓ innings Wednesday and plan to recall righty Landon Knack, Roberts said.
The Dodgers’ pitching plans for the next couple weeks are in flux.
Though right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto and left-hander Tarik Skubal have been rounding into the best versions of themselves down the stretch, Snell’s injury is the latest to deplete the ranks.
Right-hander Roki Sasaki (right middle finger blister) has been on the IL for almost three weeks. He threw a four-inning, 48-pitch live batting practice session Wednesday, with Dermabond covering the sensitive area on his finger.
The Dodgers had planned to discuss how to deploy him when he returns from the IL, but after the game, Roberts said to “make sure guys have ample rest,” his next outing will be a start.
Sasaki would be lined up to pitch against the Padres next week.
“It’s playable,” manager Dave Roberts said of Sasaki’s blister. “And given the Dermabond, the time that he’ll have in between this next outing, the hope is that it’s dang near close to being healed.”
Right-hander Tyler Glasnow hit a rough patch in his last two starts but said his back, which sidelined him for three and a half months, “feels good.” The Dodgers sent him back to Los Angeles after the series in Miami to cut down on the number of flights he’d have to sit on before his scheduled start Friday.
“Get him home, get him acclimated to Pacific Standard Time, not have to do two legs,” Roberts said. “So Tyler feels great. He’ll be ready to go on Friday.”
Roberts reiterated after the game that he’s “not concerned with Tyler,” who came out of a bullpen session Wednesday feeling “normal.”
If the Dodgers need another spot start in the next week and a half, they have right-hander Emmet Sheehan waiting in the wings. They optioned him to triple-A Oklahoma City on Monday, in favor of an extra reliever. But over his last two major-league starts, he’s limited opponents to one run and five hits in 11 ⅔ innings.

CINCINNATI — Now what?
Roki Sasaki threw 48 pitches in four simulated innings to Dodgers hitters on Wednesday afternoon, testing the blister on his right hand that landed him on the injured list. He gave up a home run to Eliezer Alfonzo but otherwise “was good,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
Sasaki threw with Dermabond on his injured finger. A surgical adhesive used to close cuts and incisions, pitchers are allowed to use it in games if their team gets permission from MLB in advance.
“He came out of it well,” Roberts said. “So we have to huddle up here and figure out what’s his role. What does it look like as we sit here on the 17th or 18th of September, whatever? So the number one most important thing is that he came out of that session well, and then now we got to figure out how to plug him in. He’s going to be important, but I just don’t know right now what role.”
Sasaki seemed destined for a bullpen role again this postseason, a role he assumed successfully last year. But the Dodgers have reason to hesitate on turning Sasaki into a reliever with Blake Snell leaving his start after just one inning on Wednesday night and Tyler Glasnow’s status.
Glasnow flew back to Los Angeles after his start in Miami. It was the second consecutive start in which Glasnow was not sharp and this time he could be seen in the dugout stretching out his back. But after the game, he said his back felt fine and Roberts said Glasnow threw a “normal” bullpen session in L.A. on Wednesday and is scheduled to make his next start on Friday night.
Sasaki is penciled in now to start during the series against the San Diego Padres in Los Angeles next week and remain a starter at least for now.
“One can argue it’s best to take down a couple starts, keep him built up, because if something does happen, he’s built up,” Roberts said. “The other side is you can assimilate him into the ’pen and get comfortable in that role – if that is the role.
“But again, I don’t want to speak out of turn and say that’s done, because it’s not.”
NO SHO
The Dodgers are about to complete their first road trip in three seasons without Shohei Ohtani. Yoshinobu Yamamoto might have missed Ohtani more than any other of his teammates.
“It’s been a weird feeling because I talk to him all the time in the clubhouse,” Yamamoto joked through his interpreter when asked about Ohtani’s absence. “All I have is Roki, but he doesn’t really talk to me.”
Back in Los Angeles, Ohtani has been receiving treatment for his knee and bicep injuries. According to Roberts, Ohtani began swinging a bat, hitting off a tee this week.
“There’s going to be a consistent build-up,” Roberts said. “Don’t know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive, and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”
Ohtani will be eligible to be activated from the IL next Wednesday. Whether he is ready to play that day or shortly after, Roberts said the expectation is that Ohtani will return in time to play before the regular season ends on Sept. 27.
“I do,” Roberts said. “Whether it happens or not is to be determined. But I do expect him to be back to play in some regular-season games. Don’t know how many of them.”
COMING/GOING
Right-hander Edwin Diaz made his fifth rehab appearance with Triple-A Oklahoma City on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless inning to close out the Comets’ playoff berth-clinching victory. Diaz did allow a double to a fellow big-leaguer on rehab, Miguel Andujar.
Meanwhile, Edgardo Henriquez returned to Los Angeles and underwent an MRI, which confirmed the diagnosis of a “low-grade back strain,” Roberts said. He won’t be eligible to pitch again in the regular season but Roberts said the Dodgers are “hopeful” he could come back for the postseason.
Left-hander Kris Bubic was activated from the 60-day IL before Wednesday’s game and right-hander Paul Gervase was returned to OKC. In order to clear a spot on the 40-man roster for Bubic, Triple-A outfielder Ryan Ward was designated for assignment.
Right-hander Landon Knack will be added to the active roster before Thursday’s game and Bobby Miller will be returned to OKC.
ALSO
Outfield prospect Charles Davalan (the 41st pick in last year’s draft) was named MVP of the Class-A Midwest League and Great Lakes manager Jair Fernandez was named the league’s Manager of the Year. Davalan hit .292 with 24 home runs and a .937 OPS. He is scheduled to play in the Arizona Fall League, where he is expected to start testing out a possible conversion to second base.
UP NEXT
Dodgers (LHP Justin Wrobleski, 11-5, 3.78 ERA) at Reds (RHP Brady Singer, 6-14, 5.38 ERA), Thursday, 9:40 a.m., SportsNet LA, 570 AM

item.content:encoded:
Shohei Ohtani’s aching right arm. Freddie Freeman’s throbbing right knee. Edwin Díaz’s disastrous form on a minor-league rehabilitation assignment.
Whatever problems surfaced in recent weeks, the Dodgers were able to convince themselves they could overcome them.
The reason: Even with Ohtani unable to pitch, they had the most talented starting rotation of this era.
Suddenly, that source of comfort is a major concern.
Blake Snell departed his start in Cincinnati on Wednesday after just one inning with what was described as a tight left groin.
Consider that Tyler Glasnow traveled directly home from Miami rather than to follow the Dodgers to Great American Ball Park for their four-game series against the Reds, and there are reasons to be worried.
Very worried.
With an inconsistent offense and combustible bullpen, the Dodgers were going to be heavily dependent on their starting pitching in the playoffs.
That rotation could now be unraveling.

The last time Snell strained his left groin was when he was pitching for the San Francisco Giants in 2024. He was sidelined for a month.
For what it’s worth, Snell is convinced this particular injury isn’t severe and plans to make his next start, according to people familiar with this situation.
“Stopped before it got too bad,” one of the people said.
Then again, weren’t similar claims once made about Ohtani?
As for Glasnow, he remains on track to pitch on Friday.
Manager Dave Roberts said Glasnow skipped the Cincinnati leg of the trip to better prepare for his starting assignment at Dodger Stadium against the San Francisco Giants.
“Get him acclimated to Pacific Standard Time,” Roberts said.
By sending Glasnow back to Los Angeles, the Dodgers spared him a three-hour flight from Miami to Cincinnati.
Glasnow was sidelined for 3 ½ months because of back problems, and Roberts intimated something could be wrong with him after his most recent start. In his last two appearances, the 6-foot-8 right-hander gave up a combined eight runs, 11 hits and seven walks in 10 innings.
The questions about Snell’s and Glasnow’s health came at a time when the rotation was coming together before the postseason.
Snell in particular was sharp after returning from an elbow cleanup that cost him three months. Before his early departure on Wednesday, Snell was 4-0 with a 1.04 earned-run average since he was activated from the injured list on Aug. 11.
Snell wasn’t the only Cy Young Award-caliber pitcher rounding into shape.
The day before Snell scaled the mound, it was Yamamoto’s turn to do so, and last year’s World Series Most Valuable Player pitched seven scoreless innings in a 4-0 win over the Reds.
The seven-inning start was the third in a row for Yamamoto, who improved his record to 14-8 and lowered his earned-run average to 2.51.
“I feel really good and I don’t have any physical problems,” Yamamoto told reporters in Japanese. “I want to treat practice each and every day with importance and go into October in the best condition.”
The opening game of the series was started by Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award winner who was acquired from the Detroit Tigers before the trade deadline.
Skubal pitched seven scoreless innings of his own in a 4-1 victory over the Reds. In his previous start, which was also against the Reds but at Dodger Stadium, Skubal pitched 7 ⅓ innings.
“Just getting in a rhythm,” Skubal said.
Just last week, the Dodgers had a playoff rotation that would have looked to other teams like the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse.
Now, there’s a chance they could be forced to send Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan to the mound in playoff games.
The Dodgers could conceivably win a championship with a rotation of Yamamoto, Skubal, Sasaki and Sheehan but that would require their offense to be productive.
How much can the Dodgers count on that, considering the physical problems Ohtani and Freeman have encountered? And how would using Sasaki as a starter instead of a reliever affect their bullpen?
Snell removed himself from his start on Wednesday so the Dodgers wouldn’t have to find out. The question is whether he did so in time. Their season depends on it.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers left-handed pitcher Blake Snell has exited Wednesday's game against the Cincinnati Reds after one inning in a concerning development with less than two weeks to go in the regular season.
Snell pitched a scoreless first inning with one strikeout across 19 pitches. There didn't appear to be anything noticeably wrong with him during the frame, but his fastball velocity was down.
At the conclusion of the first inning, Snell went down to the clubhouse alongside team trainer Thomas Albert.
Now, he's out of the game, with right-hander Blake Treinen replacing him in the bottom of the second inning.
What is Blake Snell's Injury?
The Dodgers announced Snell was removed from the game with left groin tightness.
Manager Dave Roberts will provide a more substantial update after the game, which will include whether or not Snell will need to go on the injured list.
Dodgers Can't Afford a Blake Snell Injury Right Now
Snell opened the year on the IL as he recovered from shoulder inflammation that dated back to last year. He returned for one start in May before going right back on the IL to undergo surgery to remove loose bodies in his elbow.
He missed another three months before returning in August, and has been absolutely dominant ever since.
Entering Wednesday, Snell was 4-0 with a 1.04 ERA in six starts since coming off the IL. Including Wednesday's scoreless first inning, he has 47 strikeouts over 35.2 innings and hasn't allowed a home run in that stretch.
The Dodgers are relying on Snell and fellow superstar pitchers Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tarik Skubal to carry them in October. Thus, the team will hope Snell isn't dealing with anything serious moving forward.
Who Will Replace Blake Snell in Dodgers Rotation if He's Forced to Miss Time?
The Dodgers' starting rotation is dealing with an onslaught of injury concerns as the season winds down.
While the rotation is led by Yamamoto and Skubal (who underwent midseason elbow surgery while with the Detroit Tigers), behind them is a bunch of question marks.
Tyler Glasnow has struggled since returning from a nearly four-month absence due to a back injury. Justin Wrobleski has been removed from the rotation amid his forearm injury and struggles. Roki Sasaki is currently on the IL with a blister. Eric Lauer is out for the season due to an elbow injury.
Then there's Shohei Ohtani, who won't return as a pitcher this year (and may not even be 100% as a hitter).
The Dodgers recently demoted Emmet Sheehan, but could recall him if Snell goes on the IL. He was sharp over his two September starts, allowing one run over 11.2 innings.
If Snell isn't forced to miss time, the Dodgers will take a big sigh of relief knowing their superstar trio in the starting rotation is intact with October looming. If he's forced to go on the IL, though, it will be yet another massive blow in the team's chances to three-peat.

item.content:encoded:
Edgardo Henriquez’s regular season was already effectively over once the Dodgers placed the hard-throwing pitcher on the 15-day injured list Monday with low back discomfort.
Henriquez, whose 103.6-mph fastball was the fastest pitch thrown by a Dodger since at least 2008, was diagnoesed with a low back strain. Bill Plunkett of the Southern California News Group reported Wednesday, Sept. 16, that the pitcher is “hopeful” he can return in October after getting the results of an MRI exam.
“Hopeful” and “probable” can be a world apart. In Henriquez’s case, it’s unclear whether his hope stems from the severity of his diagnosis, or from his faith that the Dodgers will play deep enough into the postseason to give him a chance to recover.
In either event, the Dodgers’ bullpen without Henriquez is a very different one than what they hoped to carry in their quest to three-peat as World Series champions.
Henriquez’s fastball touched 103.6 on June 2 in a game against the Arizona Diamondbacks, and again on Aug. 29 in a game against the Detroit Tigers.
Speed is just one facet of Henriquez’s game. His 71-to-25 strikeout-to-walk ratio, combined with only 37 hits allowed in 60 innings, gave the right-hander an at-times untouchable arsenal.
No right-handed pitcher had made more appearances for the Dodgers this season than Henriquez’s 61. Without him, manager Dave Roberts might have to get creative.
Right-hander Roki Sasaki, a starter during the regular season and a reliever during the team’s 2025 World Series run, might return in a relief role once he’s recovered from a finger blister. Edwin Diaz, who is currently on a rehab assignment of his own, struggled mightily in the closer’s role this season — but might be needed in some capacity just to get the Dodgers through to the end of the postseason.
Diaz, a three-time All-Star, had an 11.85 ERA in 16 appearances with the Dodgers before landing on the injured list with a neck injury Aug. 16.

The Los Angeles Dodgers moved closer to restoring their pitching depth before Wednesday’s series finale against the Cincinnati Reds.
Right-handed starter Roki Sasaki threw a live batting practice session at Great American Ball Park in Cincinnati. Dodgers management is hoping the session clears the last hurdle in Sasaki’s recovery from a right middle-finger blister that has sidelined him since the end of August.
A return to the active roster appears imminent, though the Dodgers haven’t decided whether he’ll resume his rotation spot or shift to the bullpen for the final weeks of the regular season.
Either way, Sasaki is expected to work exclusively out of the bullpen once the playoffs begin.
Sasaki could give manager Dave Roberts’ pitching staff a boost as the Dodgers gear up for October.
Before landing on the injured list, Sasaki posted a 4.60 ERA and 1.33 WHIP with 117 strikeouts over 119.1 innings across 23 starts. He was pulled from his Aug. 26 outing against the Atlanta Braves once the blister appeared. With a fastball averaging 97.8 mph and a plus splitter, Sasaki carries real swing-and-miss upside.
Bullpen an option
Should the Dodgers use him in the bullpen down the stretch, his triple-digit fastball and put-away splitter could bolster L.A.’s late-inning group immediately. Returning him to the rotation alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell would instead add starter depth and help manage workloads over the final two weeks of the regular season.
Keeping Sasaki’s finger healthy is a priority for the Dodgers front office, and avoiding another setback matters as the 24-year-old works his way back. Despite his inconsistent season, Sasaki has shown great stuff and figures to be a key piece of L.A.’s pitching staff as the postseason nears.
A clean live BP outing could lead to a short rehab assignment or a quicker activation before the Dodgers face the San Francisco Giants in their next series. Whether he lands in the rotation or the bullpen for the stretch run, the Dodgers will have another weapon at their disposal heading into October.

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers will be in every game they play in October, and that alone means they will enter the playoffs as the favorites to win the World Series.
Not because of Shohei Ohtani. Not because of Freddie Freeman. And certainly not because of their bullpen.
There were a number of alarming developments in the last week or so, but if any team is designed to survive them, it’s the Dodgers.
Whatever their problems, they still have the best rotation in baseball.
No player influences the outcome of a game as much as a starting pitcher, and the Dodgers are the only team that will be able to roll out one Cy Young Award-caliber arm after another after another.
The Dodgers were negligent with Ohtani, and the verdict on their management of Freeman is pending, but they at least set up their pitchers the right way.
The rotation is more than a collection of big names. In Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell, the Dodgers have three starters who are peaking in time to deliver the kinds of performances that will be required for them to win their third consecutive World Series.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto pitched seven shutout innings on Tuesday in a 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds, marking his third consecutive seven-inning start.
“I feel really good and I don’t have any physical problems,” Yamamoto told reporters in Japanese. “I want to treat practice each and every day with importance and go into October in the best condition.”
Yamamoto isn’t alone.
The day before Yamamoto’s start, Tarik Skubal pitched seven scoreless innings of his own in a 4-1 victory over the Reds. In his previous start, which was also against the Reds but at Dodger Stadium, Skubal pitched 7 ⅓ innings.
“Just getting in a rhythm,” Skubal said.
Blake Snell, who is scheduled to take his turn in the rotation on Wednesday, was 4-0 with a 1.04 earned-run average in the six games he started since returning from an elbow cleanup that cost him three months.
The one source of concern in the rotation is Tyler Glasnow, who, like Snell, was slow-played in his return from an injury. Sidelined for 3 ½ months because of back problems, Glasnow showed promise in his first couple of starts after he came back. But in his last two starts, he gave up a combined eight runs, 11 hits and seven walks in 10 innings. But as the team’s No. 4 starter, he is unlikely to start more than one game in any postseason series.
Even before Ohtani was placed on the injured list because of right arm and left knee injuries, the starting pitching was likely going to have to carry the Dodgers – much as it did last year.
Recent developments have shifted even more of the burden to the starting pitchers.
Edwin Diaz, their $69-million closer, was blow-torched for five runs in ⅔ of an inning in the most recent game of his minor-league rehabilitation assignment. At this point, he’s a longshot to make the postseason roster.
Diaz’s failure to rediscover his All-Star form will have major ramifications on the bullpen, which lost ninth-inning candidate Edgardo Henriquez to a lower-back problem for the remainder of the regular season. Henriquez’s status for the playoffs remains a mystery.
Manager Dave Roberts’ current ninth-inning choice, Tanner Scott, is in a minor slump, as he has given up runs in five of his last 12 apperances.
While the Dodgers will have to find a closer – Roki Sasaki? – their ability to create favorable matchups in the innings before the ninth is also under question. The simplest way to address those uncertainties will be for the starters to pitch deeper into games. Last year, Yamamoto pitched a complete game in the National League Championship Series and another in his next start in the World Series. Snell had an eight-inning start in the NLCS.
The greater problem could be the already-inconsistent offense, which could go into the playoffs with physically-compromised versions of Ohtani and Freeman.
Freeman missed three of five games before starting at first base on Tuesday. Freeman collected three hits in the game, but he’s 37 years old and the Dodgers can’t be certain how his right knee will hold up.
As for Ohtani, Roberts reported on Tuesday that he resumed baseball activities. Roberts said he expected Ohtani to return before the end of the regular season, but hedged his prediction.
“Whether it happens or not,” Roberts said, “is to be determined.”
If the Dodgers don’t know if Ohtani will be able to even step into the batter’s box next week, how could they possibly count on him to be a consistent source of offense?
They can’t.
In other words, the margin for error could be miniscule for the Dodgers. Their starting pitchers might have to be close to perfect. The challenge will be formidable. But considering who will be pitching for them, it will be very much in the realm of possibility.

The Los Angeles Dodgers recently sent Edwin Díaz on his second rehab assignment of the season. His first stint in Oklahoma City — back when he was rehabbing following elbow surgery — didn't go well. He posted a 10.80 ERA in just 1⅓ innings. Impossibly, however, he's been even worse his second time around.
Díaz has made four rehab outings for the so far. His first was almost spotless (he gave up a walk), but his second lasted just ⅔ innings after he gave up a run on two walks. The third was a promising bounce back — one hit, one walk, no earned runs in a full inning — but his latest was a downright disaster.
On Sunday, Diaz gave up five earned runs on two hits, a hit by pitch, and three walks. He was yanked before he could get out of the inning.
The Dodgers still have a few days before they need to make a roster move, but under no circumstances can he be used in close games, not even if they clinch a postseason berth. The Atlanta Braves are still within striking distance for a first-round bye, and the Dodgers can't afford to lose it.
When Díaz comes back, the only acceptable situation to use him in would be a blowout, and even then, fans would find it impossible to trust him. Although Tanner Scott appears to be turning back into a pumpkin, even he would lend the team greater reassurances in close games.
Edwin Díaz's latest rehab meltdown should force Dodgers to leave him off their postseason roster
It also puts the Dodgers in an uncomfortable but undeniable position: Díaz can't be on the postseason roster.
Roki Sasaki is likely to go back to the rotation when he returns from injury, but repeating his role as LA's lights-out postseason closer could be on the docket if Scott fails to prove himself trustworthy. Tyler Glasnow is also expected to move to the bullpen in October, so the Dodgers could even audition him in the role.
While the Dodgers are still the heavy favorites to win the World Series, it'll be an undeniable embarrassment to the team if they do it without Díaz — their $69 million man — who they haven't been able to figure out all season long.

Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Roki Sasaki’s regular-season status is unclear, according to Dave Roberts.
The Dodgers are trying to determine whether Sasaki will pitch again before the regular season wraps up or if his next outing will come in the postseason as a reliever.
Sasaki has been battling a blister, and he has thrown some bullpen sessions, but he is not ready to return yet, Roberts said.
Per the skipper, he will throw in a simulated game on Wednesday, September 16th, before the team decides whether he can pitch this season.
Originally, the Dodgers were hopeful Sasaki would pitch as early as Thursday, according to The Athletic’s Katie Woo, but that is no longer the case under Dave Roberts’ new timeline.
Only a handful of games remain in the regular season, and if he doesn’t pitch this week, he has only one other week left to pitch.
It seems there may not be a soft landing for the young Japanese pitcher, and he will be asked to jump headfirst into a role he is familiar with.
Why Sasaki’s setback may not be a big deal
This season, Roki Sasaki has pitched 119.1 innings in 23 games, so he will not be battling much rust.
Additionally, he hasn’t been totally shut down for long; he got treatment for the blister and has diligently ramped up his recovery.
Sasaki will not enter the postseason cold, and he has pitched out of the bullpen before, notably in the 2025 postseason when he was the closer.
While he may be asked to be the setup man rather than the closer, he should still have plenty of experience to draw on before the playoffs begin.

The Los Angeles Dodgers made Edwin Diaz the highest paid closer over the offseason. Now, he might not even make the postseason roster.
Diaz had a rehab outing Sunday in which he faced eight batters, retiring only two while walking three and hitting a batter. He threw 30 pitches to get those two outs, with only 13 strikes. Manager Dave Roberts talked about his recent woes on Monday before the Dodgers game against the Cincinnati Reds.
“He needs to pitch better. It hasn’t been good,” Roberts said on Monday. “He’s going to pitch on Wednesday, and I guess we’ll evaluate then. I think the world of him. The baseball card looks great. But where we’re at, there’s got to be something for us to be able to hang our hat on. And he knows that. He knows that. He wants to pitch well. So for me, Wednesday, we’ll be watching closely.”
He also acknowledged that Diaz might not make the postseason roster.
“Yeah … we have to go with our best pitchers, as far as performance, talent, all that stuff. So my bet is that he will be (one of them). But again, there’s got to be some kind of evidence or something for us, again, to sort of bet on. My bet is yes, but we still have to see something.”
Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic has more on the terrible season overall that Diaz has had as a Dodger here.
The Dodgers are already down another reliever, at least for the rest of the regular season. Edgardo Henriquez went on the IL on Monday with lower back discomfort. Bobby Miller was recalled from Triple-A Oklahoma City. Right-hander Paul Gervase and left-hander Kris Bubic also joined the team in Cincinnati. Gervase was added to the active roster, and Bubic could be added in the coming days.
Roki Sasaki has been sidelines with a blister and is tentatively scheduled to pitch on Thursday in Cincinnati. However, the weather is supposed to be hot and humid, and the team is worried about how that will affect Sasaki’s blister.
“We just can’t put him in a position to go backward. And so obviously people can look at Thursday. But again, if he can’t do it without accomplishing it, finishing a start, and not regress, then it’s not worth it. So I think for us, we’re just keeping it open-ended right now.”

The fresh arm express continues to run in September, with Emmet Sheehan optioned to Triple-A Oklahoma City ahead of Monday night's series opener against the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ball Park, one day after he pitched six scoreless innings on Sunday in Miami.
Paul Gervase was called up from Triple-A to give the Dodgers an extra arm in the bullpen, after the Dodgers used four relievers Friday, three on Saturday, and four more on Sunday against the Marlins. Monday is the fourth day of a stretch of 10 game days in a row for the Dodgers, their final extended stretch of games this season.
This had nothing to do with Sheehan's performance, as he allowed only one run in 11 2/3 innings last week after getting called back up from Oklahoma City himself, with 15 strikeouts. But Sheehan is on the outside looking in when it comes to the Dodgers' postseason rotation, and the team might also get Roki Sasaki at some point this week from a blister on his right middle finger.
Gervase last pitched on Friday for Oklahoma City, striking out four in a four-out save in a scoreless outing to close out a win over Sugar Land. On the season, the 6'10 right-hander had a 4.56 ERA and five saves in 38 games in Triple-A, with 66 strikeouts and 35 walks in 47 1/3 innings.
This is the fifth stint in the majors this season for Gervase, who has a 2.35 ERA in four appearances for the Dodgers, with eight strikeouts and five walks in 7 2/3 innings.
